sources.notes: Source: Poddar et al., Cureus 18(3):e104772 (2026), KIMS Bhubaneswar, Odisha; retrospective sterile-body-fluid antibiogram, Jan 2021-Dec 2022. 2307 samples, 291 isolates (12.6% positive); GPC 54%, S. aureus most common (92/291), MRSA 48.9%; K. pneumoniae top GNB (40), E. coli (27), Acinetobacter (24), Pseudomonas (19). All susceptibility data are presented ONLY as unlabeled bar charts (Fig 1 = Gram-positive: S. aureus, CONS, Enterococcus; Fig 2 = Gram-negative: K. pneumoniae, E. coli, Pseudomonas spp., Acinetobacter spp.) plus narrative sentences. There are NO numeric susceptibility tables. Method: rendered figure pages with PyMuPDF at 6x, calibrated the y-axis from detected tick-label centers (Fig 2: 0%=y1383, 100%=y368; Fig 1 baseline y1504), then extracted each bar's top and mid-bar color programmatically. Color->drug map validated by matching extracted values to the paper's own text (Acinetobacter imipenem 41.9 vs 'imipenem 41%', gentamicin 41.5 vs 'aminoglycosides 41%', cotrimoxazole 36.8 vs '37.5%', ciprofloxacin 36.8 vs '38%'; E. coli ciprofloxacin 10.8 vs 'ciprofloxacin resistance high 90%'; Pseudomonas ceftazidime 20.9 vs '21%', ciprofloxacin 9.9 vs '10-11%'). Values are %
issues: Staph aureus text-derived cells (linezolid 95.65, dapto 95, TGC 92, VA/TEI 90.21): the paper states these for 'Staphylococcus spp.' collectively (Fig 1 has separate S. aureus and CoNS bar groups). Assigning them specifically to S. aureus is a reasonable but not certain mapping; the 95.65% 'highest' value could belong to either Staph group.

Pseudomonas amikacin s=20.9 is read as LOWER than meropenem/cefepime (25.9), but the text explicitly says Pseudomonas showed 'highest sensitivity to amikacin, followed by carbapenems' — i.e., amikacin should exceed the carbapenems. Bar-read ordering is inconsistent with the text; value is approximate so not force-corrected, but flag for review.

Klebsiella ampicillin s=41.9 (bar read) is clinically implausible since K. pneumoniae is intrinsically ampicillin-resistant (expected ~0%); cannot confirm from the rendered bar chart. Possible misread of the AMP bar.
Oxacillin s=51.1 is a valid 100-R conversion from MRSA 48.9% (45/92); direction correct.

All remaining Gram-negative per-drug numbers are pixel reads off Figure 2 bar chart and cannot be independently confirmed to the stated decimal precision; they are appropriately flagged approx and are broadly consistent with the text ranges (amikacin 41-63%, carbapenems 40-60%, E. coli cipro ~10%).

sources.notes: ICMR AMRSN 2024, part A: Enterobacterales (chapter 2) and non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli (chapter 3), plus isolation counts from chapter 1. 99,027 culture-positive isolates from the network's tertiary-care centres. Enterobacterales rows are 'all specimens except urine and faeces' (spec nonurine) by location, urine rows are all locations; non-fermenter rows are 'all samples (except faeces)' (spec all) by location and by specimen. Colistin figures are percent intermediate. CR and CS rows are carbapenem-resistant and carbapenem-susceptible subsets. Isolates come from tertiary care hospitals; the report says the data do not reflect community AMR (p5). The ICMR network report for 2024 (21 regional centres; 99,027 culture-positive isolates). sources.notes: Source: Gautam et al, Indian J Med Res 2019;149:208-215 (ICMR multi-centric ESBL study, 4 tertiary centres: AIIMS Delhi, PGIMER Chandigarh, CMC Vellore, JIPMER Puducherry; Oct 2014-Mar 2016). Study covers ONLY E. coli (341 isolates) and K. pneumoniae (304 isolates) — no P. aeruginosa, A. baumannii, S. aureus, or Enterococcus. Method: Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion, CLSI. Table II reports % SUSCEPTIBLE by centre; Table III reports % RESISTANT (n/N) split by ESBL-producer vs non-ESBL. I derived OVERALL susceptibility by pooling Table III ESBL + non-ESBL resistant counts per drug (s = 100 - pooled %R, from_R:true for all pooled cells). Colistin values taken directly from the printed overall figures in the Results text (E. coli 99% = 271/274; K. pneumoniae 98% = 229/234), not from R. CAVEAT: Table III denominators (e.g. 167+202=369 for E. coli, 98+126=224 for K. pneumoniae) exceed stated collection totals of 341/304, likely reflecting drug-specific tested subsets/classification; per-drug pooled %R is nevertheless computed directly from printed n/N. Individual per-centre susceptibility values are available in Table II if centre-level breakdown is preferred. ESBL prevalence context: CDT dete

sources.notes: Ninth NARS-Net annual report: 62 sentinel sites (medical college laboratories) in 34 states and UTs, priority bacterial pathogens January to December 2025 (first isolate per patient). All figures are percent resistant (intermediate counted as not resistant). Specimens: pus aspirate (PA) is shown as pus; other sterile body fluids (OSBF) as sterile body fluids, although NARS-Net OSBF also includes CSF and broncho-alveolar lavage. Table rows combine all location types (set all). Location rows (outpatient, ward, ICU) come from bar charts with printed data labels; the report adds emergency department isolates to inpatient wards (shown here as wards). Cells marked x in the source (drug not in the panel for that specimen) are absent. Salmonella Typhi and Paratyphi A are reported separately; pefloxacin has no drug key. Candida from blood (997 isolates, fungal NRL) has no susceptibility table, so none is recorded (see excluded). The report warns that specimens come mostly from patients not responding to first-line antibiotics, which may skew resistance upward.

Tables report %RESISTANT (%R) per specimen column; ALL s-values here were converted s=100−R (from_R:true). Guidelines: CLSI. Specimen scope for each organism entry is the table's per-specimen N (BLOOD or URINE). I extracted blood (sterile-site benchmark) for all six core organisms, plus urine for E. coli, Klebsiella and Enterococcus (UTI-relevant). Tables 6–11 = S.aureus/Enterococcus/E.coli/Klebsiella/Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter. Report labels genus-level "Klebsiella species", "Pseudomonas species", "Acinetobacter species", "Enterococcus species" (species not split) — mapped to K. pneumoniae / P. aeruginosa / A. baumannii as the dominant species and to generic "Enterococcus". MRSA context: cefoxitin %R (methicillin surrogate) = 53% in blood, 43% in pus, 100% in OSBF(n=4) for S. aureus; so MRSA ~53% among blood isolates. VRE: Enterococcus vancomycin %R = 3% blood, 0.26% urine, 2% pus. Linezolid 0%R across all specimens for both S.aureus and Enterococcus. Colistin 0%R (100%S)

sources.notes: Cureus 2026 (Mohod et al.), IGGMC Nagpur; study period May 2024–April 2025; 4603 culture-positive isolates. Tables 2-4 (pages 6-8) report % RESISTANT — all s values converted as s=100-R (from_R:true). IR=intrinsic resistance, NR=not recommended by CLSI, NT=not tested, MIC=only MIC recommended, U=tested only in urinary isolates — these cells omitted or marked. E. coli/K. pneumoniae from Table 2 (lactose-fermenting GNB); P. aeruginosa/Acinetobacter from Table 3 (non-lactose-fermenters) — 'Acinetobacter spp.' mapped to Acinetobacter baumannii per scope. S. aureus/Enterococcus faecalis/faecium from Table 4. Colistin 0%R = 100%S all GNB. MRSA = 48.72% (matches S. aureus cefoxitin 48%R → 52%S). VRE 0.77%. Salmonella Typhi (n=11) figures from narrative prose on page 7 (not tabulated): ampicillin 78%R, cefotaxime 49%R, azithromycin 64%R, levofloxacin 64%R, cotrimoxazole 46%R. Nitrofurantoin/Fosfomycin tested only in urinary isolates. penicillin and high-level-gentamicin (hlg) use non-list tokens.
